name: The Great Plane of Brunswick Square

location.address: Brunswick Square Gardens, Bloomsbury, London WC1N 1AF

transport: 5 min walk from Russell Square station (Piccadilly Line)
verify_notes: Probably dates from the 1796 laying out of Brunswick Square Gardens, then the grounds of the Foundling Hospital, laid out as a green space for the Hospital's children. Well over 200 years old; reckoned the second oldest London plane in central London after Berkeley Square's planes (planted 1789, our lon_004). Named one of the ten Great Trees of London in 2008 (London Tree Forum/Paul Wood map). Coordinates from Wikipedia's Great Trees of London table (51.5242, -0.1219), tree-level per that source's convention. A March 2026 blog post (andrewwhitehead.net) carries fresh photographs confirming the tree alive and healthy, and notes it recently received its own information board in the square. No girth/height measurement found in either source; both agree independently on the c.1796 planting and the 2008 Great Tree designation.

name: The Valence Park Holm Oak

location.address: Valence Park, next to the moat at Valence House, Becontree, Dagenham, London RM8 3HT

access: Free, public park; the moat enclosure immediately beside the oak was closed for restoration works stated (2026) to complete by spring 2026, so current accessibility right up to the trunk is unconfirmed as of this pass, though the wider park stays open
transport: Becontree station (District Line) then bus 62 to Becontree Avenue/Valence Avenue, or Chadwell Heath rail station, roughly 20-25 min walk or a short bus ride either way
verify_notes: Genuine age conflict between two credible sources, not silently resolved: the Barking and Dagenham Post (quoting the borough's own Heritage Education Officer Mark Watson) says the Mertinn family, who bought the estate in the early 1700s having immigrated from Germany 50 years before and made their money in jewellery, planted the oak deliberately to make the estate look grander, putting it at roughly 340-350 years old. The London Gardens Trust's own inventory site record (ID BAD024), a more clinical survey-style source, instead dates the grounds' Holm oak and yew only to the C19th (so under roughly 225 years, some of that range overlapping the low end of the other claim). Both agree it stands beside the historic moat and is one of London's most impressive holm oaks. It was named the Valence Park Holm Oak in the Great Trees of London list roughly ten years after the October 1987 Great Storm (so circa 1997), which the tree survived unscathed while the storm felled some 15 million trees nationally; its heavily buttressed, low-spreading growth habit is credited for that survival. Coordinates are Wikipedia's Great Trees of London table entry (51.5581, 0.1350), which appears to be park-level rather than a tree-mapped pin, hence approximate. The moat restoration closure (valencehousecollections.co.uk) was stated as expected to finish by spring 2026; a later pass should confirm the enclosure has actually reopened before this ships as anything but flagged.

name: The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane
species: London Plane, Baobab Group (Platanus x hispanica)
age_estimate: roughly 100 to 200 years, exact age unknown

location.address: South of the lower grassy area, near the elm avenue, Ravenscourt Park, Hammersmith, London W6

transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)
verify_notes: Nicknamed for its huge, swollen, knobbly trunk under a small crown that looks disproportionate to it, the signature look of the rare 'Baobab' cultivar of London plane, believed to result from a viral infection rather than normal growth; comparable specimens grow in Canterbury. One of two Great Trees of London within Ravenscourt Park. Age is genuinely uncertain and no source gives a firm figure: elmparadise.blogspot.com (a specialist plane-tree blog) says estimates run from the early to late 1800s (so 150-225 years); graftingardeners.co.uk instead puts it at roughly 100 years, though noting it may date to 1812 when the estate belonged to George Scott. Flagged for that spread rather than picking one. graftingardeners.co.uk also repeats a claim, unverified elsewhere, that the tree was damaged by a WWII bomb and its odd shape comes partly from the regrowth; treat as local legend, not fact, until a second source confirms it. Alive and current as of Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society reference work, updated 2025), which records the arborist Richard Moore taking propagation cuttings from this exact tree; two of six cuttings rooted and now grow at Sculpture By The Lakes in Dorset, too young yet to show the parent's swollen form. Coordinates from Wikipedia's Great Trees of London table, tree-level per that source's convention.

name: The Fountain Court Mulberries

location.address: Fountain Court, Middle Temple, London EC4Y 9DH
location.neighbourhood: Temple, City of London / Westminster border

access: Genuinely public but restricted hours: Middle Temple's garden and Fountain Court are open to the public on weekdays roughly 12:30-3pm, excluding bank holidays, entered via the Garden Room off Middle Temple Lane; occasionally closed for high winds or private functions
transport: 5 min walk from Temple station (Circle, District Lines)
verify_notes: Two gnarled black mulberries, both leaning on wooden supports but in good health, grow either side of the 1681 fountain in Middle Temple's Fountain Court, an enclosed legal-quarter courtyard between Middle Temple Hall and the river-side gardens. Four were originally planted together and only these two survive, the other pair removed in the 1970s. Sources disagree on the exact planting year, a small but real discrepancy, never picked silently: Middle Temple's own site (an archive article about the fountain) dates the planting to 1897, for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee; an independent mulberry-history blog (sandrasgardenblog.wordpress.com) instead gives 1887, her Golden Jubilee, with the specific date of 20 June and a note that the planting was marked with a dinner in Middle Temple Hall. Either way the trees are roughly 130-140 years old. Genuinely open to the public within limited hours (12:30-3pm weekdays), the same restricted-but-real access pattern as the neighbouring Inner Temple Garden. Samuel Johnson and other literary figures associated with the Temple would have known this fountain, though not these specific trees, which postdate him by a century. No recent (2020s) photograph or news mention found confirming current condition beyond the 'in good health' line on Middle Temple's own site, undated but on a page about an ongoing feature of the court.
